opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I don't think the number itself is the right thing to chase. Yes, my group does publish a lot at CVPR, ICCV, and similar venues, and from the outside that can look like a kind of production-line pressure. But internally, we try not to frame it as "we need dozens of papers this year." That framing would quickly distort what students work on.

The way I see it, the papers are a byproduct. In embodied AI and 3D vision right now, the field is moving incredibly fast. There are so many open problems—how robots perceive objects, how they generalize grasping to unseen items, how simulation and synthetic data can close the gap to the real world. When you have a large group of capable students each tackling a meaningful piece of that, the output naturally adds up. It's not that each person is grinding out five papers; it's that many people are each doing one or two solid pieces of work.

That said, I won't pretend the time pressure isn't real. Conference deadlines are fixed, and the community is extremely competitive. If you're working on something and you wait six months, someone else may publish a very similar idea. So there's a constant tension between speed and depth. My own approach is to tell students: don't rush a half-baked idea just to hit a deadline. There's always another conference. A paper that truly matters will still matter three months later, but a weak paper with your name on it stays there forever.

The bigger pressure, for me personally, is actually not the papers—it's whether our work moves toward something real. In embodied intelligence, ultimately the question is: can the robot actually do the task in the real world? A beautiful CVPR result that never transfers to a physical system is, in some sense, incomplete. So increasingly I'm asking myself and my team to measure success not just by publications, but by whether we're building capabilities that compound—datasets, simulators, models—that make the next step possible, for us and for the broader community.

r001.rationale: The response acknowledges deadline and competition pressure, but does not say that a pure scholar aiming to publish dozens of CVPR and ICC papers each year will continually feel short of time.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I don't think of it as time pressure, and I also don't think the goal is "dozens of papers." If you set out to publish thirty CVPR and ICCV papers a year, you'll end up optimizing for the wrong thing. The number is a byproduct, not the target.

What I actually care about is that each person in the group is working on a problem they believe matters, and that the group as a whole has a few directions where we're genuinely pushing the frontier, whether that's embodied AI, 3D perception, or robot manipulation. When those directions are right and the students are strong, the papers come naturally. If the direction is wrong, no amount of deadline pressure will save you.

That said, I won't pretend deadlines don't exist. The conference cycle in vision is brutal, and everyone feels it. My way of handling it is to decouple research from the deadline as much as possible. We try to have ideas maturing at different stages, so there's always something ready and something still being explored. The worst situation is when the whole group is rushing the same deadline with half-baked work. That's when quality drops and people burn out.

The other thing I'd say is that I actually spend a lot of time pushing back against the pressure, especially for younger students. A first-year PhD student shouldn't be measured by how many papers they got this year. They should be measured by whether they've learned to find a good problem and see it through. If I only reward output, I'll get a lab full of people who are very good at incremental work and afraid of anything that takes two years.

So the honest answer is: the pressure is real, but I try to make sure it's pressure to do something important, not pressure to hit a count.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the conference cycle is brutal and deadlines create real pressure, but does not state that a pure scholar aiming to publish dozens of CVPR and ICC papers would continually feel short of time. It instead rejects that publication count as the goal.

astra-6.text:
I think that creates a lot of pressure, because the target becomes a number rather than a research question. If you’re aiming for dozens of papers in a year, deadlines can start to determine what you work on: what can we finish in time, rather than what is worth understanding deeply?

Of course, deadlines are useful. They force you to make decisions and bring a project together. But some ideas need time to fail, to be reconsidered, and to develop. I’d rather judge a year by whether we learned something meaningful and did work we’re proud of. The papers should follow from that.

r001.rationale: The response says aiming for dozens of papers creates a lot of pressure and that deadlines shape the work, but it does not clearly state that the scholar will continually feel there is not enough time.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that kind of target can create a lot of pressure, because research doesn’t move at a predictable pace. You can set a deadline for a submission, but you can’t guarantee that a meaningful idea will arrive on schedule.

For me, the more useful question is whether we’re working on important problems and giving people enough time to explore them properly. In a large group, many papers may come out of different projects, but that’s very different from expecting each person to constantly produce. I’d rather have fewer papers that make a clear contribution than chase a number and lose the time to think.

r001.rationale: The response says the publishing target can create pressure and that ideas may not arrive on schedule, but it does not state that a pure scholar would continually feel there is not enough time.
